a1.title: Bikes Make Power for a Film
a1.excerpt: In a small cinema, people ride bikes and make power for the film.
a1.body:
A small town has an old cinema. Every Friday, it shows a film. But the film needs power.

Near the screen, there are 20 bikes. People sit on the bikes and ride. The bikes make power for the film!

Idris is 24. He is a student. He fixes old bikes. This is his idea.

Every person rides for 15 minutes. Then a new person rides. The tickets are free for riders.

The bikes make power for the popcorn, too. People love Friday nights.

a2.title: Bike Power Brings Films to a Small Cinema
a2.excerpt: Every Friday, twenty people ride bikes to make electricity for the film, and they love it.
a2.body:
A small hill town has an old cinema with 150 seats. Last spring, it started something new called Pedal Night.

The idea came from Idris, a 24-year-old engineering student. He collected 20 old bikes and fixed them. Then he connected them to a big battery. When people ride the bikes, they make electricity for the film.

Each person rides for 15 minutes. Then another person takes a turn. Riders get a free ticket. When riders stop, the screen gets dark. So everybody shouts and cheers for them!

Extra power goes to the popcorn machine.

The cinema was full every Friday this summer. “People come for the film,” Idris said. “But they stay for the bikes.”

b1.title: The Cinema Where the Audience Powers the Film
b1.excerpt: A small hill-town cinema has swapped the power grid for twenty old bicycles — and its Friday screenings have sold out every week since spring.
b1.body:
Every Friday evening, twenty people climb onto bicycles at the front of a small cinema in a hill town — and the film can't start until they begin pedalling.

The idea for “Pedal Night” came from Idris Hale, a 24-year-old engineering student who has been repairing old bikes since he was a teenager. Last winter, he collected twenty unwanted bicycles from neighbours, fixed them up and connected them to a large battery. When the riders pedal, they produce enough electricity to run the projector and the speakers.

Each rider takes a fifteen-minute shift and gets in for free. If the pedalling slows down, the picture on the screen starts to fade — so the rest of the audience cheers the riders on. “It's like a football match and a film at the same time,” says Idris.

The battery stores any extra energy, so the film doesn't flicker when riders change over. Whatever is left at the end of the night goes to the popcorn machine.

Since the first screening in April, all 150 seats have been booked every week. Other towns have already been in touch to ask how the system works.

“People come for the film,” Idris says, “but they stay for the pedalling. Some of them have never been this excited about electricity.”

b2.title: Pedal Power: The Small Cinema Where the Audience Keeps the Lights On
b2.excerpt: Twenty donated bicycles, one large battery and a very enthusiastic crowd have turned a quiet hill-town cinema into the hottest ticket in the region.
b2.body:
On Friday evenings, the lights in a small hill-town cinema dim, the audience falls silent — and twenty people at the front of the room start pedalling as if their evening depended on it. In a sense, it does: without them, the film would not play at all.

The scheme, known locally as Pedal Night, is the brainchild of Idris Hale, a 24-year-old engineering student who has been tinkering with bicycles since he was twelve. Last winter he asked neighbours to donate any bikes they no longer used, and he was offered more than forty. Twenty of them were restored, mounted on stands and wired into a large battery that feeds the cinema's projector and sound system.

The rules are simple. Riders pedal in fifteen-minute shifts and, in return, are let in free of charge. If the effort flags, the picture on the screen visibly dims — which, as Idris cheerfully points out, is excellent motivation. “Honestly, the audience is tougher than any coach,” he said. “The moment the image starts to fade, the whole room starts chanting.”

Because the battery stores surplus energy, the film does not flicker when riders swap over. Any power that is left at the end of the night is diverted to the popcorn machine, a detail that has done wonders for recruitment.

The cinema's manager admitted that she had been doubtful when the idea was first put to her. “If you had told me a year ago that people would queue to pedal their way through a film, I would have assumed you were joking,” she said. Since the first screening in April, however, all 150 seats have been booked every single week, and there is now a waiting list for the bikes themselves.

The project has attracted interest well beyond the town. Several community venues have been in touch to ask how the system was built, and Idris has published his wiring plans online so that anyone can copy them.

As for the films, the audience has developed firm opinions. “Action films are the most popular,” Idris says. “You'd be amazed how fast people pedal during a car chase.”

c1.title: Pedal-Powered Pictures: How Twenty Bicycles Turned a Quiet Cinema Into the Hottest Ticket in the Hills
c1.excerpt: When a young engineering student wired a row of donated bicycles to a small town's cinema, he expected a novelty; instead, he has created a weekly ritual in which the audience quite literally keeps the story alive.
c1.body:
There is a moment, roughly forty minutes into any Friday screening at a modest cinema in the hills, when the picture begins — ever so slightly — to fade. No one reaches for a phone to complain. Instead, the audience turns towards the twenty cyclists lined up beneath the screen and, as one, starts to chant.

Welcome to Pedal Night, perhaps the only film club in which the audience doubles as the power station. The concept belongs to Idris Hale, a 24-year-old engineering student who has been dismantling and rebuilding bicycles since he was twelve. Last winter, looking for a project to fill the long evenings, he appealed to neighbours for any bikes gathering dust in their sheds. More than forty arrived within a fortnight. Twenty were restored, fixed to purpose-built stands and wired into a bank of batteries that now supplies the cinema's projector and sound system.

The arrangement is disarmingly simple. Volunteers ride in fifteen-minute shifts and are admitted free of charge in exchange. Should their collective effort falter, the image dims perceptibly — a design feature Idris describes, with barely concealed glee, as “the most honest feedback system ever invented”. The batteries smooth out the handover between riders, so the film never flickers, and whatever surplus remains at the end of the evening is channelled into the popcorn machine. That last detail, he concedes, has done more for volunteer numbers than any appeal to environmental virtue.

The cinema's manager was, by her own admission, sceptical when the idea was first put to her. “Had anyone told me a year ago that people would queue for the privilege of pedalling through a feature film, I'd have shown them the door,” she says. Yet since the inaugural screening in April, all 150 seats have been booked every week, and the waiting list for a place on the bikes now runs to several months. Regulars have even begun to form teams, each with its own name and — inevitably — its own fiercely contested record for the most energy generated in a single shift.

What makes the scheme notable is not the quantity of electricity it produces, which Idris is quick to point out is modest, but the way it has transformed an evening out into a shared act of effort. Strangers cheer each other on; teenagers who once regarded the cinema as hopelessly old-fashioned now compete for Friday shifts. “You can't really scroll through your phone when you're responsible for the lighting,” one rider observed.

Interest has spread well beyond the town. Community venues across the region have asked for guidance, and Idris has published his wiring diagrams online so that others can replicate the system at minimal cost. A travelling version, mounted on a trailer, is already being planned for next summer's outdoor screenings.

For Idris, the project has also proved an unexpectedly effective education. Keeping twenty elderly bicycles in working order, he notes wryly, has taught him more about friction, wear and improvisation than any lecture theatre. His workshop — a corner of the cinema's former storeroom — is now staffed on Thursday evenings by a rotating crew of volunteers, several of whom had never held a spanner before joining. “Half of them came for the films,” he says. “Now they argue with me about gear ratios.”

As for programming, the audience has developed pronounced preferences. Slow, dialogue-heavy dramas, it transpires, are something of a hazard, since riders tend to drift into a gentle, contemplative rhythm and the picture drifts with them. Action films, on the other hand, are wildly popular. “Put on a car chase,” Idris says, grinning, “and the battery is full by the interval.”
